The woman collects them, embarrassed as if she had just revealed her deepest secrets to the world.
Deymowa passes her and suddenly a little boy, maybe six or seven years old, runs up to her.
Looking at her with smiling eyes, very pleased with himself, he says: "Praise be to Jesus Christ!"
She responds automatically, yet solemnly: "For ever and ever, amen.

The bones of the people buried there were collected and respectfully reburied in another place.
On this occasion, the skull of Jakub Frank was removed from the grave and, carefully described as the "skull of a Jewish patriarch", ended up in the hands of Offenbach town's historian.
Many years later, under unknown circumstances, it ended up in Berlin, where it was subjected to detailed measurements and studies and identified as an example of Jewish racial inferiority.

"Quiet!" suddenly says the priest, raising a finger to listen.

Let's follow that noise.
The priest decides that the water is flowing.
Soon the priest relaxes in the carriage, stretches his legs out in front of him, and lets his eyes wander over the sea of fog.
He immediately falls into a traveling reverie, for a man thinks best when on the move.

Slowly, reluctantly, the mechanism of his mind comes to life, the gears and cogs engaging to set the drive wheels in motion, just like in the clock he has standing in his presbytery hallway back home; he paid dearly for it in Lviv.
The bell will ring in a moment.
He starts to wonder if the world might have originated from such a mist.
After all, the Jewish historian Josephus Flavius maintains that the world was created in autumn, during the autumnal equinox.
One could think so, because there were fruits in paradise; if an apple was hanging on the tree, it must have been autumn.
There is some sense in that.
But then another thought comes to him:
What kind of argument is that?
Could not an all-powerful God create such meager fruits out of season, at any time of the year?
When they reach the main road leading to Rohatyn, they join a stream of pedestrians, riders, and various types of wagons that emerge from the fog, like figures made of bread for Christmas.
It's Wednesday, market day in Rohatyn, peasant wagons full of sacks of grain, cages with poultry, all kinds of farm produce are on the move.

Between them, merchants briskly march with every possible product from their stalls, now cleverly folded and carried on their backs like yokes, only to become tables full of colorful fabrics, wooden toys, and eggs bought from villages at a quarter of the price in just a moment. .
The peasants also bring goats and cows for sale, the animals terrified by the noise, become stuck in puddles.

A speeding carriage covered with a holey tarp full of noisy Jews who are flocking to the fair at Rohatyn from all over the area flies past them, and behind it a rich coach struggles to maintain its dignity in the mist and congestion on the roadway its brightly lacquered doors are black with mud, and the footman in his blue cloak seems to be out of sorts evidently, he had not expected such chaos and is now desperately looking for an opportunity to get off this damned road.
